# 4.3 – The Equation of a Line {.unnumbered}

A linear equation connects two quantities that change at a constant rate.
You’ve explored **slope**; now you’ll see how slope and a starting value work together in the equation (y = mx + b).

:::{.objectives}

* [ ] I can identify the slope (m) and y-intercept (b) in an equation of a line.
* [ ] I can graph a line using its slope and y-intercept.
* [ ] I can describe how changing (m) or (b) changes the graph of a line.
* [ ] I can explain that (y = mx + b) and (f(x) = mx + b) mean the same thing.
:::

:::{.vocab}
{{< glink "function notation" >}}, {{< glink "linear equation" >}}, {{< glink slope >}}, {{< glink "slope-intercept form" >}}, {{< glink y-intercept >}}, {{< glink "x-intercept" >}}
:::

{{< warmup >}}
A friend says the line (y = 3x + 1) “starts at 1 and goes up 3 for every step right.”
What does **start at 1** mean on a graph? What does **up 3** mean?
:::

---

## 4.3.1 – What (y = mx + b) Means

Every non-vertical line can be written as
$
y = mx + b \quad\text{or}\quad f(x) = mx + b.
$

* (m) is the **slope** — the rate of change.
* (b) is the **y-intercept** — where the line crosses the y-axis (the value when (x=0)).

:::{.think title="Why is (b) special?"}
When (x=0), (y=b). So ((0,b)) is always on the line.
:::

**Examples (read, don’t write):**

* (f(x)=2x+1) → (m=2), (b=1).
* (y=-\tfrac12 x+3) → negative slope (falls to the right), crosses at ((0,3)).
* (f(x)=4) → (m=0) (horizontal line at (y=4)).
* (x=-2) → vertical line (not a (y=mx+b) line).

---

### 4.3.2 – Interactive: Slide (m) and (b)

Use the sliders to see how changing (m) and (b) affects the line.

* $m$ changes the **tilt** (steepness and direction).
* $b$ moves the line **up or down**.

{{< include /assets/Unit_4/slope-intercept-form-widget.html >}}

:::{.you-try-m title="Quick slider challenges"}

1. Set (m=1). Move (b) from (-4) to (+4). What stays the same? What changes?
2. Fix (b=2). Move (m) from (-3) to (+3). When does the line have no (x)-intercept?
3. With (m=-2) and (b=4), estimate (f(3)) using the graph. Then compute it exactly.
:::

:::{.remember title="Intercepts (light intro)"}

* **y-intercept:** ((0,b)) — read it straight from the equation.
* **x-intercept:** where (y=0). Solve (0=mx+b) (when (m\neq 0)) to find the (x)-value.
  We’ll use these ideas more in the next lessons.
:::

---

### 4.3.3 – Graphing from (y=mx+b)

1. Plot the **y-intercept** ((0,b)).
2. Use the **slope** (m=\dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}) to get a second point.
3. Draw the line through your points.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_3/graph_from_slope_intercept.png){width="340px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.you-try title="Graph (f(x)=-2x+4)"}
Start at ((0,4)). Go down 2, right 1. Plot a second point and draw the line.
Where are the intercepts?
:::

---

## 4.3.4 – How Changing (m) and (b) Changes the Graph

**Changing (m) (tilt/steepness):**

| Equation | Slope | What happens           |
| -------- | ----: | ---------------------- |
| (y=x+2)  |   (1) | Rises steadily         |
| (y=2x+2) |   (2) | Rises faster (steeper) |
| (y=-x+2) |  (-1) | Falls to the right     |

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_3/change_m_effect.png){width="360px" fig-align="center"}

**Changing (b) (vertical shift):**

| Equation | Intercept (b) | What happens                      |
| -------- | ------------: | --------------------------------- |
| (y=2x+1) |           (1) | Crosses y-axis lower              |
| (y=2x+4) |           (4) | Crosses y-axis higher (same tilt) |

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_3/change_b_effect.png){width="360px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.real-world title="Compare two linear rules"}
Two plans: (f(x)=30x+10) and (g(x)=20x+25).
Which starts higher? Which grows faster? For a small (x), which is cheaper?
:::

---

## 4.3.5 – Point-Slope as the Same Line (brief touch)

Sometimes you know a **point** and the **slope** but not (b). You can still describe the line:

[
y - y_1 = m(x - x_1).
]

This is the **same** line as some (y=mx+b). Solving it for (y) will match the slope and reveal the same graph.

**Example (read, don’t write):**
Through ((-2,4)) with slope (3): (y-4=3(x+2)).
This has the same graph as a (y=mx+b) line.

:::{.you-try title="Just compare the forms"}
Does (y-1=2(x-3)) have the same slope as (y=2x+4)? How can you tell without fully expanding?
:::

---

{{< practice >}}


**1. Identify (m) and (b)**
a) (y=3x-2)  b) (f(x)=-\tfrac12 x+5)  c) (y=6)

**2. Read values from an equation**
For (f(x)=-2x+4):
a) (f(0)) b) When (x=3), find (f(3)) c) Solve (0=f(x)) to find the (x)-intercept.

**3. Graph (no writing equations):**
a) (y=2x+1) b) (f(x)=-x+4).
Label intercepts on each graph.

**4. Compare lines (steepness & shift):**
Which is steeper: (y=4x+1) or (y=2x+1)?
Which crosses the y-axis higher?

**5. Point-slope as the same line (form check only):**
Does (y-3=-2(x+1)) represent a line with slope (-2)?
What is its y-intercept **approximately** (estimate from a quick sketch or mental shift), without fully expanding?

:::{.answers}

1. a) (m=3,\ b=-2)  b) (m=-\tfrac12,\ b=5)  c) (m=0,\ b=6)

2. a) (f(0)=4) (y-intercept)  b) (f(3)=-6+4=-2)  c) (0=-2x+4\Rightarrow x=2)

3. Graphs vary; intercepts:
   a) (y=2x+1): y-int ((0,1)), x-int (x=-\tfrac12)
   b) (y=-x+4): y-int ((0,4)), x-int (x=4)

4. (y=4x+1) is steeper; both cross at (y=1)

5. Yes, slope (-2) (it’s the (m) in point-slope). Intercept is a bit **above** (y=1) (exact value appears when expanded; estimate is fine here).
:::
